name: Shenzhen
title: Shenzhen Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Ships
description: UTM in Shenzhen at Yantian, Shekou and Chiwan: hull structure and scrubber piping gauging on container ships, offshore vessel UTM and ship-repair support.
h1: Hull Gauging in Shenzhen: Yantian, Shekou and the Western Port
intro: Shenzhen splits into two maritime worlds: Yantian in the east, where the largest container ships load for Europe and North America, and the western port of Shekou, Chiwan and Mawan, with feeders, offshore vessels and ship repair. The two halves need different plans: a few focused hours on scrubber lines and coamings at Yantian, or days of open access in a Shekou dock. In either case the technicians come from India to whichever side of the city the ship is on.

highlights.p: Mainline container ships at Yantian are young hulls with hard-working scrubber systems. Wash-water lines, bends, reducers and overboard penetrations are where wall loss starts, and they can be gauged within a berth window.

highlights.h: Full dockings in the western port
highlights.p: The repair facilities at Shekou take container ships, tankers, offshore units and cruise ships into dock, giving the long, open access that renewal-survey gauging and steel renewal planning need.
Hong Kong sits across the boundary with its own maritime administration. Ships and managers often move between the two, and we plan visas, passes and scopes for both sides at once.

port.h: Shenzhen: Yantian's deep water and the western port
p: Yantian International Container Terminals, in the east of the city, have deep water close to the open sea and handle mainline container services, including some of the biggest ships on the Asia–Europe and transpacific trades. Calls are short and planned to the hour, and the ships are among the newest in the fleet, many of them fitted with scrubbers. The inspection questions here are less about general hull wastage and more about specific systems: scrubber wash-water and overboard piping, sea-water lines, lashing bridges and hatch coamings carrying heavy container loads. Most of the hard choices about what to gauge on these ships are made before arrival, not on the quay.

The western port, around the Shekou peninsula on the Pearl River estuary, is busier with variety: container terminals at Shekou, Chiwan and Dachan Bay serving intra-Asia and some long-haul services, a cruise home port at Shekou, and bases for offshore vessels supporting the oil and gas fields of the South China Sea. Ship-repair facilities at Shekou take container ships, tankers, bulk carriers, offshore units and cruise ships for docking and repair, which gives the western port much longer inspection windows than Yantian ever offers. A feeder or an offshore vessel here may sit for days rather than hours.

Shenzhen's location shapes the logistics as much as the port does. Hong Kong is immediately across the boundary, so a ship calling in Shenzhen may be managed from Hong Kong, attended by class surveyors from either city and supplied through agents on both sides. Ships also anchor in the waters off the western port waiting for berths, yard slots or orders, and those anchorage periods are a practical time for pre-purchase or pre-docking gauging on ships in ballast. The result is a port where the right gauging plan depends first on which half of the city the ship is in, and only then on what kind of ship it is.

facilities.h: Gauging on both sides of Shenzhen's port
p: At Yantian the work is short and focused. The team boards with a pre-agreed list — scrubber lines, overboard penetrations, sea-water piping, deck and coaming areas — and works within the cargo window under the terminal's safety rules. In the western port the range is wider: intra-Asia container ships at Shekou and Chiwan can sometimes offer ballast tank access during longer stays, offshore vessels between charters can be gauged more completely, and ships in the Shekou repair facilities are available for full survey gauging. Offshore vessels in particular can often release tanks for proper entry, because they are not working cargo while they lie at base.

Cruise ships are a particular case. A ship turning around at the Shekou cruise terminal has a full day of passenger operations and limited technical access, but a cruise ship in dock for repairs opens its tanks, piping and hull to inspection. Cruise ship piping inspection — sewage, grey-water, ballast and sea-water lines and their tanks — is a frequent need in those dockings, because those systems corrode quickly and a leak in passenger areas is far more disruptive than one in a cargo ship's engine room.
list: Yantian International Container Terminals — scrubber wash-water and overboard piping, deck and hatch coaming gauging on mainline container ships within their berth window.
Shekou and Chiwan container terminals — feeders and regional container ships that stay longer than Yantian's mainliners, sometimes long enough to open ballast tanks.
Shekou ship-repair facilities — container ships, tankers, offshore units and cruise ships in dock; survey gauging, piping inspection and checks on renewed steel.
Offshore vessel bases in the western port — South China Sea supply and support vessels between charters, with time to open tanks and measure deck cargo areas properly.
Shekou cruise home port — limited structural and piping checks during turnaround, with full gauging deferred to a docking period.
Anchorages off the western port — ships lying in ballast while they wait for Shekou berths or yard slots; buyers' surveys and pre-docking readings by launch.

context.h: Port state control and the Shenzhen–Hong Kong cluster
p: On the mainland side of the boundary, Shenzhen's foreign-ship inspections are the job of the China Maritime Safety Administration, acting as China's Tokyo MoU authority. Hong Kong, across the boundary, runs its own maritime administration and is a separate Tokyo MoU member, so a ship that calls at both can be inspected under two administrations within days. Mainland emission control rules apply on Shenzhen's side, with open-loop discharge restricted in some areas; for mainline container ships at Yantian, the scrubber's idle or closed-loop time in Chinese waters is a good opportunity to inspect its wash-water and overboard piping.

The container trade is the heart of Shenzhen's business, and the ships calling at Yantian include many of the largest and most valuable in service. Their owners and charterers care less about general wastage, which is limited on young hulls, than about local defects: erosion and corrosion in scrubber piping, cracking at hatch coaming corners and lashing bridge supports, and wastage in sea-water lines. In the western port, older feeders, offshore vessels and ships in repair bring the more traditional renewal-survey gauging, so the two halves of the port call for quite different scopes and, often, different reporting.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Shenzhen
jobs.p: Ship inspection in Shenzhen ranges from a few targeted hours on a mainline container ship to a full docking scope in Shekou. Each job is scoped with the superintendent beforehand, and the team is mobilised from India once the berth window, the offshore vessel's stand-down or the dock date is firm enough to complete visa and access arrangements. Yantian and Shekou work can sometimes be combined in one mobilisation when the ship moves between them.
list: On a large container ship at Yantian, wall-thickness readings along the scrubber wash-water and discharge lines, concentrating on pipe bends and the shell penetration, completed inside the berth window.
Crack detection at hatch coaming corners and lashing bridge supports on a mainline container ship, combined with deck plating gauging during cargo operations.
Renewal-survey preparation on a South China Sea supply vessel lying at its western-port base: tank tops, deck cargo area plating and waterline shell measured during a planned stand-down.
Sewage, grey-water and sea-water piping gauging on a cruise ship in dock at Shekou, alongside the class surveyor's docking survey.
Pre-docking gauging of a feeder container ship at Chiwan before it enters the Shekou repair facilities, so the yard has a steel estimate in hand.

logistics: Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport serves both halves of the port, and Hong Kong International Airport is an option if the team then crosses the boundary by road or ferry, which needs a Chinese visa in addition to Hong Kong entry. Yantian and the western terminals are secure port areas, with passes and escorts arranged by the ship's agent; the repair facilities issue their own gate passes and safety induction. The mainland visa is the long-lead item for a team travelling from India, since it is issued against an invitation letter, so that process begins the moment the berth window or dock date is known.

faqs.q: What can realistically be done during a Yantian berth window?
faqs.a: A focused list. Mainline calls are short and cargo work runs continuously, so we concentrate on scrubber wash-water and overboard piping, sea-water lines, deck plating and hatch coamings, and crack detection at coaming corners and lashing bridge supports. Tanks are normally left for a docking or a longer stay elsewhere. Agreeing the list before arrival is what makes the window productive.

faqs.q: Can you work on ships in the Shekou ship repair yard?
faqs.a: Yes. In dock the scope comes from the superintendent and the class surveyor; we work through tanks and spaces as the yard opens and stages them, and issue readings daily, so the owner can settle steel and piping renewal before the ship floats out. The yard issues the team's gate passes and runs its own safety induction first.

faqs.q: Our ship is managed from Hong Kong — does that change anything for a Shenzhen job?
faqs.a: Mainly the paperwork. The technical scope is agreed with the managers wherever they sit, but the team needs Chinese visas and mainland port passes for Shenzhen, which are separate from Hong Kong entry. If the managers' agent also handles the Shenzhen call, coordination is usually simple; we need the invitation letter and passes arranged on the mainland side.

faqs.q: Why gauge scrubber piping on a young container ship?
faqs.a: Because scrubber systems can wear faster than the hull around them. Wash-water is acidic and flows at high velocity, so pipe bends, reducers, the areas downstream of valves and the overboard penetration in the shell can thin or pit within a few years of service even on a young ship. Gauging those points on a schedule, rather than waiting for a leak, lets the owner plan renewal at a convenient docking.
